newsitem.title: USA: AT&T sees flat-rate Internet access persisting.
newsitem.headline: AT&T sees flat-rate Internet access persisting.

text.p: NEW YORK, Feb 26 (Reter) - The executive in charge of AT&T Corp's Internet access service does not see the demise of the industry's "all-you-can eat" pricing model of $19.95 a month anytime soon.
Still, Tom Evslin, vice president of AT&T WorldNet, said a pricing structure may eventually evolve under which users pay extra for additional services or specialized content.

"What we will see is a $19.95 base rate, with additional services priced incrementally," Evslin told reporters on a conference call to discuss changes in AT&T's WorldNet Service pricing, which leaves the flat rate of $19.95 intact.

Earlier Wednesday, AT&T's WorldNet Service said it would begin charging its long-distance subscribers $4.95 a month for five hours of service. When WorldNet was launched a year ago, AT&T extended a special offer to its long-distance customers of five free hours a month for the first year.

"We always said it would be a one-year promotion," Evslin said. "It served its purpose of introducing many people to the Internet. Things were very different a year ago. Now you can't turn on a sports event without seeing the URL of each team," he said, referring to World Wide Web site addresses known as universal resource locators (URLs).

Evslin said there was one development that could change the $19.95 flat-rate pricing model, which has been adopted by most of the Internet-access and online services industry. He cited efforts by regional Bell operating companies to seek approval from regulators to begin charging access fees for data calls, in the same manner that they charge long-distance carriers for access to local lines.
"That would end $19.95 in a hurry," he said.
Evslin declined to say whether AT&T's WorldNet Service had become profitable after one year in operation and with more than 750,000 subscribers.
To be sure, he said, "we can be profitable with $19.95" flat-rate pricing because AT&T was not encumbered by hefty subscriber acquisition costs, in contrast with its rivals.

"We don't expect to go to carpet bombing or to television campaigns," he said, in a jab at America Online Inc which has been a target of industry jokes as it has blanketed the U.S. with free floppy disks of its service software.

AT&T also made indirect references to AOL and its network congestion problems, as subscribers have swamped its service since it adopted flat-rate pricing. AT&T said it challenged other service providers to match its performance.

Still, analysts said that AT&T has fewer subscribers than America Online, whose customers tend to be heavy Internet users. AT&T said its subscribers averaged more than 10 hours a month online. AOL now has about eight million members.
Analysts also said that AT&T's subscriber count was lower than forecast after a much-hyped launch that had prospective users clamoring for software the company could not initially provide.

"It's safe to say they must be disappointed with their subscriber growth," said Gregory Wester, a research director at the Yankee Group. "They have a 60 percent share of the long-distance market and a single-digit share of Internet access."
